grid.name: ldem_site07_5m
grid.label: LOLA 5 m site model Site07 (peak near Shackleton)

classes.label: precision lander
classes.figure: pinpoint landing within an accuracy of 100 m
classes.basis: ASSUMED: 99 % of touchdowns within 100 m. The figure: JAXA calls "pinpoint landing within an accuracy of 100m" the main mission of SLIM, and reports touchdown "approximately 55m east of the original target landing site" (JAXA press release, 25 Jan 2024, read 15 Nov 2026). Treating 100 m as the 99 % radius of a circular Gaussian is this project's choice.

suggestion.why: No aim point within 200 m does clearly better (by at least 1 percentage point, beyond the sampling range).

classes.label: CLPS-class lander
classes.figure: one landing about 820 feet (250 m) from its intended site
classes.basis: ASSUMED: one standard deviation of 250 m. The figure: NASA reports IM-2 "on its side about 820 feet from the intended landing site, Mons Mouton" (NASA news release, 7 Mar 2025, read 15 Nov 2026); 820 feet is 250 m. One landing is not a statistic; taking its miss as one standard deviation of a circular Gaussian is this project's choice.

suggestion.why: Aim points within 200 m that do better for slope lose the slip margin (5 tried), so none is suggested.

classes.label: unguided lander
classes.figure: a prime landing site of 4 km x 2.4 km
classes.basis: ASSUMED: a lander with no terrain-relative navigation, as an ellipse of 670 m by 400 m. The figure: ISRO lists Chandrayaan-3's "Landing Site (Prime) 4 km x 2.4 km" (ISRO Chandrayaan-3 details page, read 15 Nov 2026). Taking a third of that area's half-axes as one standard deviation is this project's choice, and Chandrayaan-3 itself was guided. The direction of the long axis is not known, so every direction is tried.

suggestion.why: No aim point within 200 m does clearly better (by at least 1 percentage point, beyond the sampling range).

near.encoding: row by row from the top of the map grid; tenths of a degree; 255 = no 5 m terrain

wide.encoding: row by row from the top of the map grid; tenths of a degree; 255 = no 5 m terrain

picture.pole_note: screen x to the right, screen y down; the arrow points toward the south pole

limits: Boulders and small craters are invisible here: 5 m terrain shows nothing smaller than about 10 m. A lander can still come down on a rock or in a small crater that this terrain does not show.
The three lander sizes are this entry's assumptions, each tied to one public figure, not a model of any real lander.
NASA's 8° is how far the lander may lean. Ground slope is not the same thing: a footpad on a rock can tilt it more.
Only two 16 km squares near Shackleton have 5 m terrain here. Everywhere else 80 m terrain is far too coarse for the ground under a lander, so no chance is given.
The ±2° figures shift every slope the same way at once. Real errors vary from place to place, so the truth is most likely between the two.

source.limit: NASA, Human Landing System (HLS) Requirements Document, HLS-RQMT-001, initial release, 27 September 2019, requirement HLS-R-0071 Landing Site Vertical Orientation: "The HLS shall provide vertical orientation of 0 to 8° (threshold) and 0 to 5° (goal) from local vertical for surface operations."
source.limit_file: Attachment_F_-_Requirements.zip, file 'HLS-RQMT-001 SRD Rev R 20190927.pdf', page 37 of 315 (HLS-R-0021 is on page 32)
source.limit_note: NASA's number limits how far the lander may lean. Published site studies (Wueller et al. 2026; Kring et al. 2023) use it as a limit on the slope of the ground, and so do we.
source.accuracy: Same document, HLS-R-0021: the lander must come down within 100 m (3-sigma) of the target.
source.study: Wueller, L. et al. (2026), JGR Planets 131(3), e2025JE009434, section 2.2: landing areas with slopes under 8° on the LOLA 20 m grid, and at least 100 m from steeper ground.
source.baseline: NASA HLS solicitation attachment A20, Lunar Landing Site Characterization White Paper (2019): LOLA 5 m data show slopes of about 6° over a 10 m baseline.

robust_pick.how: Touchdown points are drawn at random around the aim point, as far out as each lander's accuracy says. At each one the slope is measured as in the flat-enough check: a flat plane fitted to the 5 m terrain of a 10 m square, about a lander's width. The chance is the share of touchdown points where that slope is 8° or less (5° or less for NASA's goal).
